$comment: Copy this file to claude-web.config.json and edit it, then run ./deploy.sh.
claude-web.config.json is gitignored so your settings never get committed.
Only domainName and hostedZoneName are required; everything else has a
working default. Every key can also be set as an environment variable —
see ENV_MAP in infra/config.js. Full reference: docs/DEPLOY.md.
SECURITY: read docs/SECURITY.md before exposing this to the internet.
Claude runs shell commands on this machine, so the login password is the
boundary between the internet and a shell on your box.
$comment_optional_dns: hostedZoneId skips a Route53 lookup at synth time. Leave it empty to have
the zone resolved by name. certificateArn reuses an existing ACM
certificate; leave it empty and a DNS-validated one is created for you.
$comment_profile: Named AWS profile for the CLI. Empty uses the default credential chain.
$comment_auth: 'password' is self-contained: a 32-character password is generated into
Secrets Manager and exchanged for a signed session cookie. Nothing else to
'oidc' moves authentication to the load balancer, so no unauthenticated
request ever reaches the instance. It requires an OAuth app with your
provider and all six oidc fields below.
READ THIS BEFORE CHOOSING oidc. The load balancer AUTHENTICATES — it proves
the caller holds an account with your provider — and then forwards the
request. It does not AUTHORIZE. With Google, 'has an account' is every
Google account in existence, and what is behind the door here is a shell.
So allowedEmails is the setting that actually protects the deployment: put
the addresses you sign in with, and nothing else. Both the deploy and the
chat service refuse to start in oidc mode without it.
allowedDomain is for a provider that owns a domain — Google Workspace, or a
Cognito pool you control. Never use it with a public provider: a domain you
do not control is not a restriction.
scope must contain 'email'. The allowlist matches on the email claim, so
without that scope the provider returns nothing to match against.
Endpoints for Google, GitHub and Cognito are in docs/DEPLOY.md.
$comment_network: Who can reach the load balancer at all. ['0.0.0.0/0'] is the whole
internet, which is what the login gate is for. If you only ever use this
from known networks, narrowing this is the single highest-value hardening
step available — it removes the login page from public reach entirely.
$comment_instance: t4g.large is 2 vCPU / 8 GiB on Graviton. Sizes in GiB.
$comment_admin: false attaches only what the app needs: Bedrock invoke, its own secrets,
its own volume. true adds AdministratorAccess so the workspace can deploy
other AWS infrastructure the way your laptop can — and means one leaked
password is account takeover, because Claude executes commands here.
$comment_claude: permissionMode 'bypassPermissions' lets Claude run commands without asking,
which is the intended experience and also the main risk. 'acceptEdits'
auto-applies file edits but prompts for commands; 'plan' confirms first.
effortLevel is low|medium|high|xhigh|max, and every deploy writes it over
whatever the box had — so this file is the answer, not the first deploy's.
$comment_pwa: Which set of home screen icons the installable app ships with. Directory in
this repository, relative to its root: 'pwa-icons' is the default set, and a
subdirectory of it is a set of your own, e.g. 'pwa-icons/ribbon'. It must
contain every file pwa/manifest.webmanifest names — a deploy refuses
otherwise, because an icon that 404s is an app that cannot be installed.
Only worth changing if you run more than one deployment of this repository:
they are two apps on one phone, and the icon is how you tell them apart.
$comment_git: Author on commits Claude makes in the workspace.
$comment_landing: Optional public marketing site (the landing/ directory), served from a
private S3 bucket behind CloudFront. Entirely separate from the workspace:
its own stack, its own hostname, no shared resources, and no route to the
instance. Leave domainName empty and none of it is created.
It must NOT be the same hostname as domainName above — one DNS record
cannot point at both CloudFront and the load balancer.
certificateArn must live in us-east-1, the only region CloudFront reads
certificates from. Leave it empty to have one created there for you; a
wildcard covering your zone can be reused if it is already in us-east-1.
Deploy with ./deploy-landing.sh, which is independent of ./deploy.sh.
$comment_security: Optional account-level audit trail and threat detection, as its own stack.
Deploy with ./deploy-security.sh, which is independent of ./deploy.sh and
touches nothing the workspace depends on.
cloudTrail creates a multi-region trail with log file validation, writing to
a private bucket. This is what makes the blast radius knowable: Claude runs
shell commands with the instance role's credentials, and without a trail the
only record of what those credentials did is CloudTrail's 90-day Event
history, which is not durable, not integrity-validated and not exportable.
The first question after any incident — 'what did it touch?' — has no answer.
The bucket is RETAINed on stack deletion, deliberately: 'cdk destroy' must
not delete the evidence of whatever prompted the teardown.
guardDuty is false by default because AWS allows exactly ONE detector per
account per region and CDK cannot adopt an existing one, so turning this on
in an account that already has one fails the deploy. Check with
'aws guardduty list-detectors' — an empty list means you can enable it.
logRetentionDays applies to the trail logs. 0 keeps them forever.
$comment_deployFrom: The machine full deploys are driven from. Strongly recommended.
A full deploy must not run on the instance this stack manages. Applying a
UserData change stops that instance, so everything the deploy does after
'cdk deploy' — pushing the app, checking it still requires a login — dies
with the box, and the stack goes green over an app that was never updated.
./deploy.sh refuses when it detects it is running there.
Anything else will do: a laptop, CI, or a small instance kept for the job.
Fill this in and ./deploy-remote.sh resets that machine's clone to
origin/main and runs the deploy there over SSM — which also means the
deploy survives your browser, your network or the workspace restarting.
It needs the SSM agent running, a clone of this repository with its own
claude-web.config.json, and a role that can deploy the stack. Leave
instanceId empty and ./deploy-remote.sh tells you this is what to set.
